items.meaning: To initiate conversation in a new or awkward social situation, making people feel more comfortable.
items.example: It's always a bit tricky to break the ice at these networking events, isn't it?
items.plain: It's always a bit tricky to start conversations at these networking events.
items.note: Commonly used when meeting new people; implies a slight initial awkwardness.

items.meaning: A common, friendly way to ask someone about their current experience or progress during the day.
items.example: Hi Sarah, how's your day going so far? Anything interesting happening?
items.plain: Hi Sarah, how is your day so far? Anything interesting happening?
items.note: A very common and informal greeting, suitable for colleagues or acquaintances.

items.meaning: A polite and warm expression used when introduced to someone for the first time.
items.example: Oh, you're Mark from the London office? Lovely to meet you!
items.plain: Oh, you're Mark from the London office? It's nice to meet you!
items.note: Standard polite greeting; can be used at the beginning or end of a first conversation.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask someone why they are at a particular event or location.
items.example: So, what brings you here to the conference this year?
items.plain: So, why are you at the conference this year?
items.note: Good for starting conversations with strangers at events; can be slightly formal.

items.meaning: Introduces a related topic that just came to mind because of the previous conversation point.
items.example: Oh, you mentioned the new project. Speaking of which, have you heard about the latest update?
items.plain: You mentioned the new project. Have you heard about the latest update?
items.note: A smooth way to transition topics; often used to add a new piece of information.

items.meaning: Used to transition to a new, related topic or to conclude a discussion point.
items.example: The weather's been great for cycling. On that note, I'm thinking of getting a new bike.
items.plain: The weather's been great for cycling. I'm thinking of getting a new bike.
items.note: Can be used to smoothly change direction or wrap up a segment of conversation.

items.text: if you don't mind me asking
items.form: If you don't mind me asking
items.meaning: A polite way to introduce a potentially personal or sensitive question, seeking permission first.
items.example: If you don't mind me asking, how long have you been working in this department?
items.plain: How long have you been working in this department?
items.note: A polite softener for questions; shows respect for the other person's privacy.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a question, implying it's for general interest rather than a specific need.
items.example: Just out of curiosity, how did you get into this line of work?
items.plain: How did you get into this line of work?
items.note: Makes a question sound less intrusive and more conversational.

items.meaning: To start an activity or process, especially one that involves other people.
items.example: Let's get the ball rolling on planning the team outing for next month.
items.plain: Let's start planning the team outing for next month.
items.note: Informal and common in professional settings for initiating tasks.

items.meaning: To meet someone you know after a period of time and talk about what has happened.
items.example: It was great to catch up with you at the conference; we should do it again soon.
items.plain: It was great to talk to you at the conference; we should do it again soon.
items.note: Implies a desire to reconnect and share recent life updates.

items.meaning: A common greeting used when you haven't seen someone for a while, asking about their well-being.
items.example: Hi Tom, long time no see! How have you been?
items.plain: Hi Tom, long time no see! How are you?
items.note: Used after a period of absence; invites a brief update on their life.

items.meaning: An informal greeting used when encountering someone you haven't seen for a considerable period.
items.example: Oh, Mark! Long time no see! How have things been?
items.plain: Oh, Mark! I haven't seen you in a long time! How have things been?
items.note: Very common and friendly; implies a pleasant surprise at the reunion.

items.text: what have you been up to
items.form: What have you been up to
items.meaning: An informal question asking what someone has been doing recently.
items.example: It's been a while! What have you been up to since we last met?
items.plain: It's been a while! What have you been doing since we last met?
items.note: Encourages a brief summary of recent activities or life events.

items.meaning: A common, informal response to 'How are you?' or 'How's it going?', meaning things are fine.
items.example: How's work going? Can't complain, really; it's been busy but good.
items.plain: How's work going? It's going well, really; it's been busy but good.
items.note: A casual, positive, and understated response; implies satisfaction.

items.meaning: An informal and modest response to 'How are you?', indicating things are reasonably good.
items.example: How was your weekend? Not too bad, actually; I got a lot done.
items.plain: How was your weekend? It was good, actually; I got a lot done.
items.note: A common, understated positive response, often used in British English.

items.meaning: Taking all factors and circumstances into account; despite various challenges.
items.example: All things considered, the project launch went quite smoothly.
items.plain: Despite various challenges, the project launch went quite smoothly.
items.note: A useful phrase for offering a balanced perspective or summary.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a frank or sincere statement, sometimes implying a slight hesitation.
items.example: To be honest, I'm not entirely sure what the next steps are.
items.plain: I'm not entirely sure what the next steps are.
items.note: A common discourse marker; can soften a negative or uncertain statement.

items.meaning: A slightly more emphatic way to introduce a sincere or candid opinion, often a mild criticism.
items.example: If I'm being honest, I found the presentation a bit confusing.
items.plain: I found the presentation a bit confusing.
items.note: Adds a touch more emphasis than 'to be honest'; can soften a critical remark.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that confirms or corrects something previously said, or adds detail.
items.example: Are you new here? As a matter of fact, I just started last week.
items.plain: Are you new here? I just started last week.
items.note: Adds emphasis or a slight surprise to the information being shared.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a new topic or a piece of information that is not directly related to the current one.
items.example: I'm heading to the coffee machine. By the way, did you finish that report?
items.plain: I'm heading to the coffee machine. Did you finish that report?
items.note: A very common and informal way to change the subject or add an afterthought.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a new topic or thought that has been triggered by the current conversation.
items.example: You mentioned the new software. That reminds me, I need to update my system.
items.plain: You mentioned the new software. I need to update my system.
items.note: A natural way to shift topics smoothly based on a previous comment.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a new point that is related to what was just discussed.
items.example: We were talking about travel. On the subject of holidays, where are you going this year?
items.plain: We were talking about travel. Where are you going on holiday this year?
items.note: A slightly more formal way to transition topics than 'speaking of which'.

items.text: to cut a long story short
items.form: To cut a long story short
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are going to give only the main points of a longer explanation.
items.example: To cut a long story short, we ended up missing our flight but still made it to the meeting.
items.plain: We ended up missing our flight but still made it to the meeting.
items.note: Useful for summarizing quickly when you sense the listener's attention waning.

items.meaning: Used to ask for a reminder of the last point discussed after an interruption or digression.
items.example: Sorry, my phone rang. Where were we before that?
items.plain: Sorry, my phone rang. What were we talking about before that?
items.note: Helps to smoothly resume a conversation after a pause or interruption.

items.meaning: Used to return to a previous topic after a digression.
items.example: Anyway, getting back to the budget, have we finalized the figures?
items.plain: Anyway, about the budget, have we finalized the figures?
items.note: A clear signal that you want to refocus the conversation.

items.text: I was just about to say
items.form: I was just about to say
items.meaning: Used to express agreement or indicate that you were thinking the same thing.
items.example: You're right, we should definitely try that. I was just about to say the same thing!
items.plain: You're right, we should definitely try that. I was thinking the same thing!
items.note: Shows strong agreement and a sense of shared thought.

items.meaning: Used to express complete and enthusiastic agreement with someone's statement or opinion.
items.example: That's a brilliant idea for the new campaign. I couldn't agree more!
items.plain: That's a brilliant idea for the new campaign. I completely agree!
items.note: A strong and polite way to show full agreement.

items.meaning: Used to indicate understanding of someone's point, even if you don't fully agree.
items.example: I see what you mean about the challenges, but I think we can overcome them.
items.plain: I understand your point about the challenges, but I think we can overcome them.
items.note: A useful phrase for acknowledging another's perspective without necessarily endorsing it.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that someone has made a valid or insightful observation.
items.example: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a good point.
items.plain: I hadn't thought of it that way. That's a valid observation.
items.note: Shows you are listening and value the other person's contribution.

items.meaning: Used to express reluctant or hesitant agreement, or a lack of strong conviction.
items.example: Do you think we should reschedule? I suppose so, if everyone else is busy.
items.plain: Do you think we should reschedule? Yes, if everyone else is busy.
items.note: Indicates mild agreement, often with a hint of resignation or indifference.

items.meaning: Used to express doubt or mild disagreement without being confrontational.
items.example: I'm not so sure that's the best approach for this particular client.
items.plain: I doubt that's the best approach for this particular client.
items.note: A polite way to express reservations or a differing opinion.

items.meaning: A formal and polite way to express disagreement, often used in more serious discussions.
items.example: While I respect your view, I beg to differ on the feasibility of that plan.
items.plain: While I respect your view, I disagree on the feasibility of that plan.
items.note: Quite formal; use with caution in casual small talk, but good for polite disagreement.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement of disagreement or criticism in a polite and deferential manner.
items.example: With all due respect, I think we need to reconsider the budget allocation.
items.plain: I think we need to reconsider the budget allocation.
items.note: Often signals that a polite but firm disagreement is coming; can sound slightly formal.

items.meaning: Used to soften a potentially critical or controversial statement, ensuring it's not taken personally.
items.example: No offense, but I think your idea might be a bit too ambitious for our current resources.
items.plain: I think your idea might be a bit too ambitious for our current resources.
items.note: Informal; often used before a mild criticism or a direct statement.

items.meaning: Used to clarify a previous statement, ensuring it's not misunderstood or taken negatively.
items.example: I like the new office, don't get me wrong, but the commute is a nightmare.
items.plain: I like the new office, but the commute is a nightmare.
items.note: Helps to balance a negative comment with a positive one, or prevent misinterpretation.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to say no or to deliver bad news.
items.example: Can you make it to the meeting tomorrow? I'm afraid not, I have another commitment.
items.plain: Can you make it to the meeting tomorrow? No, I have another commitment.
items.note: A common softener for negative responses; sounds more polite than a direct 'no'.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to say yes, often to something undesirable.
items.example: Is the deadline still Friday? I'm afraid so, there's no extension.
items.plain: Is the deadline still Friday? Yes, there's no extension.
items.note: Used when confirming something unpleasant; softens the impact of the news.

items.meaning: Used to express surprise at an unexpected connection or coincidence with someone.
items.example: You know my old boss? It's a small world, isn't it?
items.plain: You know my old boss? What a coincidence!
items.note: A common and friendly expression for shared acquaintances or unexpected links.

items.meaning: Used to express surprise when two unrelated things happen at the same time or are connected.
items.example: We both ordered the same drink! What a coincidence!
items.plain: We both ordered the same drink! That's surprising!
items.note: A natural reaction to unexpected similarities or events; good for light conversation.

items.meaning: Used to ask someone for their opinion or experience of something.
items.example: You've been here a month now, how do you find working in the new office?
items.plain: You've been here a month now, what do you think of working in the new office?
items.note: A polite way to solicit an opinion or assessment; slightly more formal than 'what do you think'.

items.meaning: Used to ask someone for their opinion or interpretation of something, often something new or unusual.
items.example: Have you seen the new proposal? What do you make of it?
items.plain: Have you seen the new proposal? What do you think of it?
items.note: A common way to ask for an opinion, especially on something that requires thought.

items.meaning: A polite and casual way to introduce a question or a thought you're considering.
items.example: I'm just wondering if you've had a chance to look at those figures yet.
items.plain: Have you had a chance to look at those figures yet?
items.note: Softens a direct question, making it sound less demanding.

items.meaning: A very polite and indirect way to ask a question or make a request.
items.example: I was wondering if you might be free for a quick chat later today.
items.plain: Are you free for a quick chat later today?
items.note: Excellent for making requests or asking questions very politely.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask if someone has specific information, implying they might not.
items.example: Do you happen to know if the coffee machine is working today?
items.plain: Is the coffee machine working today?
items.note: Softens a direct question, making it less demanding and more conversational.

items.meaning: A polite and common way to ask for information or directions.
items.example: Excuse me, could you tell me where the nearest exit is?
items.plain: Excuse me, where is the nearest exit?
items.note: A standard polite request for information, suitable for strangers.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to state that you don't have the requested information.
items.example: Do you know when the next train is? I'm afraid I don't know.
items.plain: Do you know when the next train is? I don't know.
items.note: A polite refusal to a question, softening the directness of 'I don't know'.

items.text: I'm afraid I can't help you
items.form: I'm afraid I can't help you
items.meaning: A polite and regretful way to say you are unable to assist someone.
items.example: I'm looking for Mr. Smith. I'm afraid I can't help you, he's not in today.
items.plain: I'm looking for Mr. Smith. I can't help you, he's not in today.
items.note: A polite way to decline a request or indicate inability to assist.

items.meaning: A polite and warm phrase used to express enjoyment of someone's company or a shared experience.
items.example: Well, it's been a pleasure chatting with you, but I really must go.
items.plain: Well, I enjoyed chatting with you, but I really must go.
items.note: A common and polite way to end a conversation, especially with new acquaintances.

items.text: it was nice talking to you
items.form: It was nice talking to you
items.meaning: A common and polite phrase used to end a conversation, expressing enjoyment of the chat.
items.example: Right, I should let you get back to it. It was nice talking to you!
items.plain: Right, I should let you get back to it. I enjoyed talking to you!
items.note: A standard and friendly way to conclude a conversation gracefully.

items.meaning: A common and polite way to signal that you need to leave a conversation or place.
items.example: It's getting late, so I should get going now. See you next week!
items.plain: It's getting late, so I need to leave now. See you next week!
items.note: A gentle way to initiate the end of a conversation without being abrupt.

items.meaning: An informal and direct way to say you need to leave.
items.example: Well, I must be off now, I have an appointment. Great to see you!
items.plain: Well, I need to leave now, I have an appointment. Great to see you!
items.note: Slightly more direct than 'I should get going', but still polite.

items.meaning: A polite way to end a conversation, implying the other person might be busy or need to leave.
items.example: You look busy, so I'll let you go. Catch up soon!
items.plain: You look busy, so I'll end our conversation. Catch up soon!
items.note: Shows consideration for the other person's time; often used on the phone.

items.meaning: A common and friendly farewell, wishing someone well.
items.example: It was good to see you. Take care!
items.plain: It was good to see you. Goodbye and be well!
items.note: A versatile and warm closing, suitable for most informal situations.

items.meaning: An informal and friendly farewell, wishing someone a good day, evening, or experience.
items.example: Right, I'm off to lunch. Have a good one!
items.plain: Right, I'm off to lunch. Have a good day!
items.note: Very common in American English; a casual and positive way to say goodbye.

items.meaning: An informal farewell, implying you expect to see the person again soon, but not at a specific time.
items.example: I'm heading out. See you around the office!
items.plain: I'm heading out. I'll see you again soon in the office!
items.note: Common among colleagues or neighbors; implies regular, informal encounters.

items.meaning: To maintain communication with someone, usually after a period of not seeing them regularly.
items.example: It was great catching up. Let's keep in touch!
items.plain: It was great catching up. Let's stay in contact!
items.note: Expresses a desire to continue the relationship; often used when parting ways.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge that a significant amount of time has passed since you last saw someone.
items.example: Wow, Sarah! It's been a while since we last met.
items.plain: Wow, Sarah! A long time has passed since we last met.
items.note: A common and friendly opening when reuniting with someone.

items.meaning: A general and friendly inquiry about someone's overall well-being and current situation.
items.example: Hey Mark, how's everything going with the new project?
items.plain: Hey Mark, how is the new project progressing?
items.note: A broad question that invites a general update on their life or work.

items.meaning: An informal question asking for recent updates or news in someone's life.
items.example: It's good to see you! What's new with you these days?
items.plain: It's good to see you! What has happened in your life recently?
items.note: A common way to invite someone to share recent events or news.

items.meaning: A common, informal response to 'What's new?' or 'What have you been up to?', meaning not a lot.
items.example: What have you been up to? Nothing much, just the usual work and home routine.
items.plain: What have you been up to? Not a lot, just the usual work and home routine.
items.note: A casual, understated response, often used when there's no significant news.

items.meaning: An informal response indicating that things are continuing as usual, without much change.
items.example: How's life? Oh, you know, same old same old. Busy as ever.
items.plain: How's life? Oh, you know, things are continuing as usual. Busy as ever.
items.note: Very informal; implies a routine or predictable situation.

items.meaning: An informal response indicating that things are normal and routine, without anything special.
items.example: What are you up to this weekend? Just the usual, some errands and relaxing.
items.plain: What are you up to this weekend? Just the normal things, some errands and relaxing.
items.note: A casual way to say nothing out of the ordinary is happening.

items.meaning: A slightly more emphatic version of 'can't complain', indicating things are genuinely good.
items.example: How's business? Can't complain really, things are picking up.
items.plain: How's business? Things are good, things are picking up.
items.note: A common, positive, and understated response, often used in British English.

items.meaning: Used to describe a period of intense activity, busyness, or stress.
items.example: How's work? It's been hectic lately with all the new projects.
items.plain: How's work? It's been very busy lately with all the new projects.
items.note: A common way to explain a lack of free time or energy.

items.meaning: Used to express optimism that a situation is improving or will improve.
items.example: After a tough quarter, things are looking up for the company.
items.plain: After a tough quarter, the company's situation is improving.
items.note: A positive and hopeful phrase, good for sharing good news or optimism.

items.meaning: Used to express hope that something will happen as desired.
items.example: I've got an interview tomorrow, so fingers crossed!
items.plain: I've got an interview tomorrow, so I hope it goes well!
items.note: A common, informal expression of hope or good luck.

items.meaning: Used to ward off bad luck after mentioning something good or positive.
items.example: The project is going smoothly, touch wood, we haven't had any major issues.
items.plain: The project is going smoothly, we haven't had any major issues.
items.note: Common in British English; equivalent to 'knock on wood' in American English.

items.meaning: Used to ward off bad luck after mentioning something good or positive.
items.example: My car hasn't broken down in years, knock on wood!
items.plain: My car hasn't broken down in years, I hope it continues that way!
items.note: Common in American English; equivalent to 'touch wood' in British English.

items.meaning: Used to state that something is so obvious that it does not need to be said.
items.example: It goes without saying that we need to prioritize customer satisfaction.
items.plain: We obviously need to prioritize customer satisfaction.
items.note: Emphasizes the self-evident nature of a point; can sound slightly formal.

items.text: to make a long story short
items.form: To make a long story short
items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are going to give only the main points of a longer explanation.
items.example: To make a long story short, we decided to go with the original plan after all.
items.plain: We decided to go with the original plan after all.
items.note: A common way to summarize quickly, similar to 'to cut a long story short'.

items.meaning: Used to introduce your personal opinion, often one that might be slightly critical or unsolicited.
items.example: If you ask me, they should have started this project months ago.
items.plain: They should have started this project months ago.
items.note: Can sound a bit direct or opinionated; use with care in very formal settings.

items.meaning: Used to introduce your personal viewpoint or opinion on a matter.
items.example: From my perspective, the new policy will create more efficiency.
items.plain: I think the new policy will create more efficiency.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to offer an opinion, emphasizing it's one view.

items.meaning: Used to introduce your personal opinion, often implying that others might disagree.
items.example: As far as I'm concerned, the meeting was a complete waste of time.
items.plain: I think the meeting was a complete waste of time.
items.note: Can sound quite strong or definitive; use when you have a firm opinion.

items.meaning: A casual and polite way to introduce an opinion or an estimate.
items.example: I'd say we're looking at about three more weeks to complete this phase.
items.plain: I think we're looking at about three more weeks to complete this phase.
items.note: Softens an opinion or estimate, making it sound less assertive.

items.meaning: Used to express a tendency to agree with someone, often after some consideration.
items.example: After hearing your points, I'm inclined to agree with your assessment.
items.plain: After hearing your points, I tend to agree with your assessment.
items.note: A polite and thoughtful way to express agreement, often after deliberation.

items.meaning: Used to express a tendency to believe something, often after some consideration.
items.example: Given the data, I'm inclined to think we should proceed with caution.
items.plain: Given the data, I tend to think we should proceed with caution.
items.note: A polite and thoughtful way to express an opinion or belief.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty or a lack of complete knowledge about something.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure what the best solution is for this problem.
items.plain: I don't know what the best solution is for this problem.
items.note: A polite way to admit uncertainty, softer than a direct 'I don't know'.

items.meaning: Used to express doubt or a lack of full belief in an idea or argument.
items.example: I'm not entirely convinced that this strategy will yield the desired results.
items.plain: I doubt that this strategy will yield the desired results.
items.note: A polite way to express skepticism or mild disagreement.

items.meaning: A common and friendly question to ask someone about their recent weekend activities.
items.example: Good morning! How was your weekend? Did you do anything fun?
items.plain: Good morning! What did you do this weekend? Did you do anything fun?
items.note: A standard conversation starter on a Monday or after a break.

items.meaning: A casual way to ask if there's any interesting news or events in someone's life.
items.example: Hey, long time no see! Anything exciting happening with you lately?
items.plain: Hey, long time no see! Is there any interesting news with you lately?
items.note: An informal way to invite someone to share recent positive news.

items.meaning: A common question to ask about someone's upcoming activities or intentions.
items.example: It's almost Friday! What are your plans for the weekend?
items.plain: It's almost Friday! What will you do this weekend?
items.note: A good way to keep a conversation going by looking ahead.

items.meaning: A polite way to introduce a request or action that might inconvenience someone.
items.example: I hope you don't mind, but I borrowed your stapler for a moment.
items.plain: I borrowed your stapler for a moment.
items.note: Softens a request or an admission of a minor transgression.

items.meaning: Used to explain why you are contacting someone, usually to see how they are or if they need anything.
items.example: Hi, I was just checking in to see how you're getting on with the report.
items.plain: Hi, I wanted to see how you're getting on with the report.
items.note: A casual and considerate way to initiate contact or follow up.

items.meaning: A direct but polite way to ask for someone's opinion or emotional response to something.
items.example: How do you feel about the new changes to the company policy?
items.plain: What's your opinion on the new changes to the company policy?
items.note: Invites a more personal or emotional response than 'what do you think'.

items.text: it's been a pleasure meeting you
items.form: It's been a pleasure meeting you
items.meaning: A polite and warm phrase used to express enjoyment of meeting someone for the first time.
items.example: Well, I must be going. It's been a pleasure meeting you, Sarah.
items.plain: Well, I must be going. I enjoyed meeting you, Sarah.
items.note: A standard and polite way to end a first-time conversation.

items.meaning: An informal farewell, meaning you will see or speak to the person again at a later time.
items.example: I'm off to a meeting now, I'll catch you later!
items.plain: I'm off to a meeting now, I'll see you later!
items.note: Very common and casual, suitable for colleagues or friends.

items.meaning: Used to describe a day where a lot of work or tasks were successfully completed.
items.example: I'm ready to head home; it's been a productive day.
items.plain: I'm ready to head home; I got a lot done today.
items.note: A positive and professional way to summarize the day's work.

items.meaning: A friendly and informal way to ask someone about their general well-being and current circumstances.
items.example: Hey, stranger! How's life treating you these days?
items.plain: Hey, stranger! How are things going for you these days?
items.note: A warm and slightly more personal greeting, often used with friends.

items.meaning: A friendly and open question asking someone what they are thinking or worrying about.
items.example: You seem a bit quiet today. What's on your mind?
items.plain: You seem a bit quiet today. What are you thinking about?
items.note: Shows concern and invites a deeper conversation, if appropriate.

items.text: I was just thinking about you
items.form: I was just thinking about you
items.meaning: Used to express a pleasant coincidence when you encounter someone you were just thinking of.
items.example: Oh, hi! I was just thinking about you and that project.
items.plain: Oh, hi! I was just thinking about you and that project.
items.note: A warm and friendly way to start a conversation, implying a connection.

items.meaning: An informal expression of surprise at seeing someone unexpectedly in a particular place.
items.example: Well, fancy meeting you here! I didn't expect to see you at this event.
items.plain: I'm surprised to see you here! I didn't expect to see you at this event.
items.note: Common in British English; expresses pleasant surprise at an unexpected encounter.

items.meaning: Used to express happiness or delight at an unexpected event or encounter.
items.example: Oh, it's you! What a pleasant surprise to see you here.
items.plain: Oh, it's you! I'm happy to see you here unexpectedly.
items.note: A warm and positive reaction to an unexpected meeting or good news.

items.text: I'm glad we ran into each other
items.form: I'm glad we ran into each other
items.meaning: Used to express pleasure at an unplanned meeting with someone.
items.example: I'm glad we ran into each other; I've been meaning to ask you something.
items.plain: I'm glad we met unexpectedly; I've been meaning to ask you something.
items.note: A friendly way to acknowledge an unplanned meeting and open conversation.

items.meaning: A direct but polite question asking about the source of someone's information or acquaintance.
items.example: You know Sarah? How do you know her?
items.plain: You know Sarah? Where did you meet her?
items.note: Common for finding common ground or understanding connections.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are only in a place temporarily, not staying long.
items.example: I can't stay long, I'm just passing through on my way to another meeting.
items.plain: I can't stay long, I'm only here temporarily on my way to another meeting.
items.note: Useful for setting expectations about your availability in a conversation.

items.meaning: Used to politely inform someone that you will arrive after the scheduled time.
items.example: Sorry, I'm running a bit late for our coffee chat.
items.plain: Sorry, I will be a bit late for our coffee chat.
items.note: A common and polite apology for tardiness.

items.meaning: Used to promise to provide updates or new information as it becomes available.
items.example: I don't have all the details yet, but I'll keep you posted.
items.plain: I don't have all the details yet, but I'll give you updates.
items.note: A common and reassuring phrase for ongoing situations.

items.meaning: Used to invite someone to inform you about a specific condition or need.
items.example: Let me know if you need any help with that presentation.
items.plain: Tell me if you need any help with that presentation.
items.note: A polite and helpful way to offer assistance or request information.

items.meaning: Used to express anticipation and excitement for a future event or activity.
items.example: I'm looking forward to the team building event next month.
items.plain: I'm excited about the team building event next month.
items.note: A positive way to express enthusiasm for future plans.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a long period has passed since a particular event occurred.
items.example: It's been a while since we last had lunch together.
items.plain: We haven't had lunch together for a long time.
items.note: A gentle way to suggest reconnecting or reminiscing.

items.meaning: Used to turn a question back to the other person after you've answered it yourself.
items.example: I had a great weekend, how about you?
items.plain: I had a great weekend, what about your weekend?
items.note: A simple and effective way to maintain conversational flow.

items.meaning: A common and direct way to ask for someone's opinion or thoughts on a topic.
items.example: The new coffee machine is great, what do you think?
items.plain: The new coffee machine is great, what's your opinion?
items.note: A versatile phrase for inviting participation and opinions.

items.meaning: Used to soften a question, implying it's for general interest rather than a specific need.
items.example: I'm just curious, how did you manage to finish that so quickly?
items.plain: How did you manage to finish that so quickly?
items.note: Similar to 'just out of curiosity', makes a question less intrusive.

items.meaning: Used to express happiness or relief about something positive someone has said.
items.example: You got the promotion? I'm glad to hear that!
items.plain: You got the promotion? That makes me happy!
items.note: A common and polite way to respond positively to good news.

items.meaning: Used to express sympathy or regret about something negative someone has said.
items.example: Your project got delayed? I'm sorry to hear that.
items.plain: Your project got delayed? That's unfortunate.
items.note: A common and polite way to respond with empathy to bad news.

items.text: it's been a pleasure working with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.meaning: A polite and professional phrase used to express enjoyment of a collaborative work experience.
items.example: As I'm leaving, I wanted to say, it's been a pleasure working with you all.
items.plain: As I'm leaving, I wanted to say, I enjoyed working with you all.
items.note: A standard and warm farewell in a professional context.

items.meaning: Used to promise to contact someone again in the future.
items.example: I'll look into that for you and I'll be in touch soon.
items.plain: I'll look into that for you and I'll contact you soon.
items.note: A common and professional way to end a conversation with a promise of follow-up.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a point that balances or mitigates a previous statement, often acknowledging another perspective.
items.example: To be fair, the project had a very tight deadline, which made things challenging for the team.
items.plain: The project had a very tight deadline, which made things challenging for the team.
items.note: A common softener, used to introduce a mitigating factor or a balanced view.

items.meaning: Used to ask for agreement or to introduce a slightly unusual or metaphorical way of describing something.
items.example: The new policy is a paradigm shift, if you will, in how we approach customer service.
items.plain: The new policy is a paradigm shift in how we approach customer service.
items.note: Adds a touch of formality or self-awareness when using a strong or slightly unusual term.

items.meaning: Used to offer an opinion or piece of information that may or may not be helpful or important.
items.example: For what it's worth, I heard they're planning to open a new coffee shop on the corner.
items.plain: I heard they're planning to open a new coffee shop on the corner.
items.note: A humble way to offer information or an opinion, suggesting it might not be highly significant.

items.meaning: Used to politely ask for more specific information or to confirm understanding of something said.
items.example: Just to clarify, are we meeting at 9 AM or 9:30 AM tomorrow for the presentation?
items.plain: Are we meeting at 9 AM or 9:30 AM tomorrow for the presentation?
items.note: A polite way to seek precision, often used in professional or semi-formal settings.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a piece of information that the speaker believes to be true, but isn't entirely certain of.
items.example: If I recall correctly, the deadline for that report was actually next Friday, not this Friday.
items.plain: The deadline for that report was actually next Friday, not this Friday.
items.note: A polite way to offer information while acknowledging a slight possibility of error.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a statement is generally true, despite some exceptions or minor details.
items.example: On the whole, the conference was a great success, even with a few minor technical glitches.
items.plain: The conference was a great success, even with a few minor technical glitches.
items.note: Summarizes a general impression, often used when giving an overall assessment.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a practical, approximate principle or guideline, not a strict rule.
items.example: As a rule of thumb, always double-check your work before submitting it to the client.
items.plain: Always double-check your work before submitting it to the client.
items.note: Implies practical advice based on experience, not a formal regulation.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that contrasts with or qualifies what was just said.
items.example: The new software is quite complex; having said that, it offers powerful features once you learn it.
items.plain: The new software is quite complex, but it offers powerful features once you learn it.
items.note: A common discourse marker for introducing a concession or counterpoint.

items.meaning: Similar to "having said that," it introduces a contrasting or qualifying point.
items.example: The weather was terrible for our trip. That being said, we still managed to have a good time.
items.plain: The weather was terrible for our trip, but we still managed to have a good time.
items.note: Interchangeable with "having said that," often used to soften a previous negative statement.

items.meaning: Used to rephrase something in a simpler or clearer way, or to explain its true meaning.
items.example: The new system is designed for optimal user experience; in other words, it's very intuitive.
items.plain: The new system is designed for optimal user experience; it's very intuitive.
items.note: Useful for clarifying or simplifying a previous statement for better understanding.

items.meaning: A polite way to offer an opinion or observation, often when it might be slightly critical or bold.
items.example: That was a rather ambitious goal, if I may say so, given the limited resources we had.
items.plain: That was a rather ambitious goal, given the limited resources we had.
items.note: Adds politeness and a touch of deference when expressing a potentially sensitive opinion.

items.meaning: Used to ensure that there is no misunderstanding about what is being said or agreed upon.
items.example: Just to be clear, we're aiming for completion by Friday, not just starting the final review.
items.plain: We're aiming for completion by Friday, not just starting the final review.
items.note: Emphasizes the need for precise understanding, often used in professional contexts.

items.meaning: A polite way to check if you have accurately grasped what someone has said.
items.example: If I understand correctly, you're suggesting we pivot to a different marketing strategy.
items.plain: You're suggesting we pivot to a different marketing strategy.
items.note: Shows active listening and seeks confirmation, useful for avoiding miscommunication.

items.meaning: Used to rephrase something in a different manner, often to make it clearer or emphasize a point.
items.example: The project is behind schedule; to put it another way, we need to accelerate our efforts significantly.
items.plain: The project is behind schedule; we need to accelerate our efforts significantly.
items.note: Offers an alternative phrasing, useful for clarity or emphasis.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you have changed your mind or reconsidered a previous statement or decision.
items.example: I'll have the chicken salad. On second thought, maybe I'll go for the pasta instead.
items.plain: I'll have the chicken salad. Maybe I'll go for the pasta instead.
items.note: Common in informal settings when making a quick change of mind.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a piece of information that is relevant or surprising in the current context.
items.example: I was just thinking about that. As it happens, I have some news regarding the budget.
items.plain: I was just thinking about that. I have some news regarding the budget.
items.note: Often used to reveal a coincidence or a piece of timely information.

items.meaning: Used to add more specific or exact information to a previous statement.
items.example: The meeting starts at 10 AM, to be precise, in Conference Room B.
items.plain: The meeting starts at 10 AM in Conference Room B.
items.note: Adds a level of detail or exactness, often used in professional communication.

items.meaning: Used to state something clearly and officially, often to ensure it is noted or remembered.
items.example: For the record, I did submit my report before the deadline, despite the technical issues.
items.plain: I did submit my report before the deadline, despite the technical issues.
items.note: Implies a desire for accuracy and official acknowledgment, can be slightly formal.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a contrasting or opposite aspect of a situation or argument.
items.example: The new office is closer to home. On the flip side, the rent is significantly higher.
items.plain: The new office is closer to home, but the rent is significantly higher.
items.note: Informal way to present a counterpoint or a different perspective.

items.meaning: Used to qualify a statement, indicating it is true only partially or up to a certain degree.
items.example: The new policy will help, to some extent, but it won't solve all our problems.
items.plain: The new policy will help partially, but it won't solve all our problems.
items.note: A common softener, used to express partial agreement or limited impact.

items.meaning: Used to qualify a statement, suggesting it is true in one way but perhaps not entirely or literally.
items.example: The project was a success, in a sense, though we didn't meet all our initial targets.
items.plain: The project was a success, though we didn't meet all our initial targets.
items.note: A softener that acknowledges a partial truth or a specific interpretation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that the information being given is based on the speaker's current knowledge, which may be incomplete.
items.example: As far as I know, the meeting is still scheduled for Tuesday morning.
items.plain: The meeting is still scheduled for Tuesday morning.
items.note: A common way to qualify information, showing awareness of potential gaps in knowledge.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a piece of information that the speaker believes to be true, but isn't entirely certain of.
items.example: If I'm not mistaken, you used to work for a competitor a few years back.
items.plain: You used to work for a competitor a few years back.
items.note: A polite way to offer information while acknowledging a slight possibility of error.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a statement that is obvious or expected, often to emphasize its importance.
items.example: Needless to say, the success of the event depends heavily on everyone's participation.
items.plain: The success of the event depends heavily on everyone's participation.
items.note: Similar to "it goes without saying," but not in the bank. Slightly more formal.

items.meaning: Used to suggest that the reality of a situation is much more extreme or serious than the words used to describe it.
items.example: The presentation was a disaster, to put it mildly; the projector didn't even work.
items.plain: The presentation was a disaster; the projector didn't even work.
items.note: An understatement, implying the situation was worse than described.

items.meaning: Used to check if the listener understands or agrees with what is being implied rather than explicitly stated.
items.example: The new system is a bit clunky, you know what I mean, not very user-friendly.
items.plain: The new system is a bit clunky, not very user-friendly.
items.note: Informal, seeks implicit agreement or understanding, often used when describing something vaguely.

items.meaning: Used to check if the listener understands an indirect suggestion or implication.
items.example: We need to be more proactive with our clients, if you catch my drift, before they look elsewhere.
items.plain: We need to be more proactive with our clients before they look elsewhere.
items.note: Informal, implies a subtle or indirect message, often used to avoid being too direct.

items.meaning: Used to state something clearly and officially, often to ensure it is noted or remembered.
items.example: Just for the record, I did submit my report before the deadline, despite the technical issues.
items.plain: I did submit my report before the deadline, despite the technical issues.
items.note: Slightly more informal than "for the record," but serves the same purpose of clarity.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a direct and honest opinion, often one that might be critical or sensitive.
items.example: To be perfectly frank, I don't think that approach will yield the results we're hoping for.
items.plain: I don't think that approach will yield the results we're hoping for.
items.note: Emphasizes honesty, can sound quite direct, use with caution in sensitive situations.

items.meaning: Used to introduce one side of a two-sided argument or consideration.
items.example: On the one hand, the new policy offers flexibility, but on the other hand, it creates confusion.
items.plain: The new policy offers flexibility, but it creates confusion.
items.note: Always paired with "on the other hand" (or implied), for presenting balanced views.

items.meaning: Used to introduce the contrasting or opposing side of an argument or consideration.
items.example: The new policy offers flexibility, but on the other hand, it creates confusion for some staff.
items.plain: The new policy offers flexibility, but it creates confusion for some staff.
items.note: Always paired with "on the one hand" (or implied), for presenting balanced views.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are going to get straight to the main point without unnecessary details.
items.example: To cut to the chase, we need to secure additional funding to complete the project on time.
items.plain: We need to secure additional funding to complete the project on time.
items.note: Informal, used when you want to get to the point quickly, often in a slightly impatient tone.

items.meaning: Used to clarify or explain a previous statement, often because it was misunderstood or unclear.
items.example: I said it was challenging. What I mean is, it requires a lot of dedication and problem-solving.
items.plain: I said it was challenging. It requires a lot of dedication and problem-solving.
items.note: A common way to rephrase or elaborate on a point for clarity.

items.meaning: Used to introduce an important point, explanation, or problem that needs to be considered.
items.example: The thing is, we don't have enough resources to take on another big client right now.
items.plain: We don't have enough resources to take on another big client right now.
items.note: Informal, often used to explain a difficulty or a crucial aspect of a situation.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the most important idea or message being conveyed.
items.example: We can debate the details, but the point is, we need to act quickly to avoid further delays.
items.plain: We can debate the details, but we need to act quickly to avoid further delays.
items.note: More direct than "the thing is," used to highlight the core message.

items.meaning: Used to soften a statement or opinion, implying it's just an observation and not a strong demand.
items.example: Maybe we should consider other options. I'm just saying, it's worth exploring alternatives.
items.plain: Maybe we should consider other options; it's worth exploring alternatives.
items.note: Informal, often used to offer a suggestion without being pushy.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you intend to speak for only a short time.
items.example: I'll be brief, but I wanted to share a quick update on the project's progress.
items.plain: I wanted to share a quick update on the project's progress.
items.note: Polite and efficient, often used at the start of a short intervention.

items.meaning: Used to resume a previous point or narrative after an interruption or digression.
items.example: As I was saying, the new marketing campaign is set to launch next month.
items.plain: The new marketing campaign is set to launch next month.
items.note: Polite and common, used to smoothly pick up a thread of conversation.

items.meaning: A polite way to interrupt someone to add a point or ask a question.
items.example: If I may interject, I have a quick question about the budget allocation.
items.plain: I have a quick question about the budget allocation.
items.note: Formal and polite, used to politely break into a conversation.

items.meaning: Used to offer a suggestion or idea tentatively, without strong conviction.
items.example: Maybe we could try a different approach, just a thought, but it might save time.
items.plain: Maybe we could try a different approach, it might save time.
items.note: Informal and humble, used to float an idea without demanding it be taken seriously.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a tentative statement or question, expressing uncertainty.
items.example: I'm not sure if this is the right time, but I wanted to discuss the upcoming project.
items.plain: I wanted to discuss the upcoming project.
items.note: A polite softener, useful for introducing a potentially sensitive topic.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a piece of information that suddenly came to mind and is relevant.
items.example: I almost forgot, the client called earlier and left a message for you.
items.plain: The client called earlier and left a message for you.
items.note: Informal, used to add a piece of information that was nearly overlooked.

items.meaning: Used to briefly summarize the main points that have been discussed so far.
items.example: Just to recap, we've agreed on the budget and the initial project timeline.
items.plain: We've agreed on the budget and the initial project timeline.
items.note: Useful for ensuring everyone is on the same page, often in meetings or discussions.

items.meaning: A polite way to contribute an additional point or piece of information to a discussion.
items.example: If I may add, the market research also indicates a strong demand for this feature.
items.plain: The market research also indicates a strong demand for this feature.
items.note: Formal and polite, used to contribute to a conversation without interrupting rudely.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a direct and honest opinion, often one that might be critical or sensitive.
items.example: To be frank with you, I think we need to reconsider our approach to this problem.
items.plain: I think we need to reconsider our approach to this problem.
items.note: Emphasizes honesty, can sound quite direct, use with caution in sensitive situations.

items.meaning: Used to introduce unwelcome or negative news or an opinion, softening the impact.
items.example: I'm afraid to say, the budget for the new initiative has been significantly cut.
items.plain: The budget for the new initiative has been significantly cut.
items.note: A polite softener for delivering bad news or a negative assessment.

items.meaning: Used to introduce positive or welcome news, expressing pleasure.
items.example: I'm happy to say, we've successfully secured the funding for the next phase of the project.
items.plain: We've successfully secured the funding for the next phase of the project.
items.note: A polite way to deliver good news, expressing personal satisfaction.

items.text: if I may be so bold
items.form: If I may be so bold
items.meaning: A very polite and formal way to introduce a potentially daring or presumptuous suggestion or question.
items.example: If I may be so bold, perhaps we should consider a complete overhaul of the current system.
items.plain: Perhaps we should consider a complete overhaul of the current system.
items.note: Very formal, used when offering a strong opinion or suggestion that might challenge the status quo.

items.meaning: Used to explain your intention or purpose, often to justify an action or question.
items.example: I'm just trying to understand the rationale behind this sudden change in direction.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the rationale behind this sudden change in direction.
items.note: A common softener, used to explain one's motives in a non-confrontational way.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a frank and honest statement, often one that might be surprising or slightly negative.
items.example: I'm not going to lie, the presentation was a bit dull, but the content was solid.
items.plain: The presentation was a bit dull, but the content was solid.
items.note: Informal, emphasizes honesty, often used before a slightly critical or unexpected remark.

items.meaning: Used to acknowledge someone's perspective or circumstances, often to defend or explain their actions.
items.example: To be fair to John, he was under immense pressure to deliver the results quickly.
items.plain: John was under immense pressure to deliver the results quickly.
items.note: A diplomatic way to offer a mitigating explanation for someone's behavior.

items.meaning: Used to explain that you are confirming something, often to avoid errors or misunderstandings.
items.example: I'm just making sure I have the correct version of the document before I start editing.
items.plain: I need to confirm I have the correct version of the document before I start editing.
items.note: A polite way to double-check information, often in a professional context.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission to leave or to briefly step away from a conversation.
items.example: If you'll excuse me, I need to make a quick phone call before the meeting starts.
items.plain: I need to make a quick phone call before the meeting starts.
items.note: A polite and common way to temporarily or permanently exit a conversation.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that you are on the verge of doing something.
items.example: I'm just about to send out the meeting agenda, so let me know if you have any last-minute points.
items.plain: I'm sending out the meeting agenda soon, so let me know if you have any last-minute points.
items.note: Useful for indicating immediate future actions, often in a helpful context.

items.meaning: Used to express pleasure or satisfaction about something you have just learned.
items.example: I'm pleased to hear that your project is progressing so well and on schedule.
items.plain: Your project is progressing so well and on schedule, which makes me happy.
items.note: A slightly more formal alternative to "I'm glad to hear," expressing satisfaction.

items.meaning: A formal way to deliver bad news, expressing sorrow or reluctance.
items.example: I regret to inform you that your application for the grant was not successful this time.
items.plain: Your application for the grant was not successful this time.
items.note: Very formal and serious, used for official bad news.

items.meaning: Used to deliver positive news, expressing pleasure or satisfaction.
items.example: I'm happy to report that our team exceeded all sales targets for the last quarter.
items.plain: Our team exceeded all sales targets for the last quarter.
items.note: A slightly formal way to deliver good news, often in a professional context.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal way to state an inability to do something.
items.example: I'm unable to provide a definitive answer on that matter until I consult with legal.
items.plain: I cannot provide a definitive answer on that matter until I consult with legal.
items.note: More formal than "I can't," used to politely decline or state a limitation.

items.meaning: A polite way to express that you must do something, often implying reluctance or a necessity.
items.example: I'm afraid I have to cut our conversation short; I have another appointment.
items.plain: I have to cut our conversation short; I have another appointment.
items.note: A polite softener for ending a conversation or stating an unavoidable obligation.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly more formal way to express that you must do something.
items.example: I'm afraid I must leave now to catch my train, but it was lovely chatting.
items.plain: I must leave now to catch my train, but it was lovely chatting.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to excuse oneself from a conversation.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't fully understand what someone is saying.
items.example: I don't quite follow your reasoning for that decision; could you elaborate a bit?
items.plain: I don't understand your reasoning for that decision; could you elaborate a bit?
items.note: A polite and common way to ask for clarification without sounding rude.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't fully understand what someone is saying.
items.example: I'm not sure I follow your logic on that point; could you explain it differently?
items.plain: I don't understand your logic on that point; could you explain it differently?
items.note: Similar to "I don't quite follow," used to politely request further explanation.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't fully grasp a concept or statement.
items.example: I'm not sure I understand the implications of that new regulation for our department.
items.plain: I don't understand the implications of that new regulation for our department.
items.note: A polite way to admit confusion and invite further explanation.

items.meaning: A polite way to express disagreement without being confrontational.
items.example: I'm not sure I agree with the proposed timeline for the project; it seems a bit ambitious.
items.plain: I don't agree with the proposed timeline for the project; it seems a bit ambitious.
items.note: A common softener for expressing a differing opinion respectfully.

items.meaning: A polite way to express doubt about one's ability to do something.
items.example: I'm not sure I can commit to that deadline, given my current workload.
items.plain: I doubt I can commit to that deadline, given my current workload.
items.note: A polite softener for declining a request or expressing a limitation.

items.text: I'm not sure I want to
items.form: I'm not sure I want to
items.meaning: A polite way to express reluctance or hesitation about doing something.
items.example: I'm not sure I want to take on another big responsibility right now, to be honest.
items.plain: I'm hesitant to take on another big responsibility right now.
items.note: A polite way to express disinclination without being blunt.

items.meaning: A polite way to express mild disapproval or dislike.
items.example: I'm not sure I like the new color scheme for the website; it feels a bit too bright.
items.plain: I don't like the new color scheme for the website; it feels a bit too bright.
items.note: A polite softener for expressing a negative opinion about something.

items.meaning: A polite way to express hesitation or unease about a situation or topic.
items.example: I'm not sure I'm comfortable discussing my personal finances in a public setting.
items.plain: I'm uneasy discussing my personal finances in a public setting.
items.note: A polite way to set boundaries or express discomfort.

items.meaning: A polite way to express that you feel unprepared or unwilling to do something yet.
items.example: I'm not sure I'm ready to take on a management role just yet; I need more experience.
items.plain: I don't feel prepared to take on a management role just yet; I need more experience.
items.note: A polite way to express hesitation about a new challenge or commitment.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate unfamiliarity with a piece of information or a person.
items.example: I'm not sure I've heard about that new initiative; could you tell me more?
items.plain: I haven't heard about that new initiative; could you tell me more?
items.note: A polite way to admit lack of knowledge and invite further explanation.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate unfamiliarity with something visual or a document.
items.example: I'm not sure I've seen the updated project timeline; is it available online?
items.plain: I haven't seen the updated project timeline; is it available online?
items.note: A polite way to admit lack of visual information and request it.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't recall meeting someone before.
items.example: I'm not sure I've met you before; my name is Sarah, I work in marketing.
items.plain: I don't recall meeting you before; my name is Sarah, I work in marketing.
items.note: A polite way to initiate an introduction or re-introduction.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't recall having a particular experience or item.
items.example: I'm not sure I've had the chance to review those figures yet; I'll check my inbox.
items.plain: I don't recall reviewing those figures yet; I'll check my inbox.
items.note: A polite way to admit something hasn't been done or experienced.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate uncertainty about possessing something or understanding.
items.example: I'm not sure I've got all the necessary documents for the application.
items.plain: I'm uncertain if I have all the necessary documents for the application.
items.note: A polite way to express doubt about having something.

items.text: I'm not sure I've got it
items.form: I'm not sure I've got it
items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that you don't fully understand something.
items.example: Could you explain that again? I'm not sure I've got it completely.
items.plain: Could you explain that again? I don't understand it completely.
items.note: Informal, used to politely ask for re-explanation.

items.text: I'm not sure I've got time
items.form: I'm not sure I've got time
items.meaning: A polite way to express that you are busy or have limited availability.
items.example: I'm not sure I've got time for a long discussion right now, but I can spare a few minutes.
items.plain: I might not have time for a long discussion right now, but I can spare a few minutes.
items.note: A polite way to manage expectations about your availability.

items.text: I'm not sure I've got the energy
items.form: I'm not sure I've got the energy
items.meaning: A polite way to express that you are tired or lack the enthusiasm for something.
items.example: I'm not sure I've got the energy for another late-night brainstorming session tonight.
items.plain: I might not have the energy for another late-night brainstorming session tonight.
items.note: Informal, used to politely decline due to fatigue or lack of enthusiasm.

items.text: I'm not sure I've got the patience
items.form: I'm not sure I've got the patience
items.meaning: A polite way to express that you are feeling impatient or easily annoyed.
items.example: I'm not sure I've got the patience for another round of revisions on this document.
items.plain: I might not have the patience for another round of revisions on this document.
items.note: Informal, used to politely express frustration or a limit to one's tolerance.

items.text: I'm not sure I've got the right idea
items.form: I'm not sure I've got the right idea
items.meaning: A polite way to express uncertainty about one's understanding or approach to something.
items.example: I'm not sure I've got the right idea about how to tackle this complex problem.
items.plain: I'm uncertain about how to tackle this complex problem.
items.note: A polite way to express doubt and invite input or clarification.
